Honest answer: **yes — I would take the “for” side**, but only if the tax is genuinely narrow: a federal inheritance tax on **extremely large estates**, not a general tax on ordinary Swiss families.

For your debate, the strongest version is:

> **Switzerland should introduce a federal inheritance tax on very large estates, because extreme inherited wealth should not become dynastic privilege financed by the rest of society.**

## Your core “for” argument

Switzerland already has a system where wealth can be passed on almost unchanged across generations. That creates a society where some people start life with a massive financial advantage, while others start with student debt, rent burdens, and uncertainty.

A federal inheritance tax on **really big estates** is not about punishing rich people. It is about saying: **your inherited wealth can be part of your private fortune, but it also has to contribute to the collective foundations that made that wealth possible — rule of law, education, infrastructure, stable currency, old-age security, and so on.**

This is especially relevant in Switzerland because:

1. **Wealth inequality is already high.**  
   A federal tax on very large inheritances targets the top slice, not the middle class.

2. **Cantonal inheritance taxes are not enough.**  
   Cantons can compete on tax rates and create differences. A federal element on extreme estates would reduce arbitrage and prevent the very rich from benefiting from cantonal competition.

3. **It can help finance the social state.**  
   Switzerland needs to pay for AHV/old-age security, health care, housing support, education, and climate adaptation. A tax on extreme inherited wealth is a reasonable contribution from those who benefit most from stability and continuity.

4. **It is less economically distortive than many other taxes.**  
   If the threshold is high enough, it barely touches normal families and small businesses. It is not a tax on work, on ordinary saving, or on middle-class pensions.

## Strong debate framing

Use this line early:

> “We are not debating whether Swiss families should be taxed when a relative inherits a home, a pension, or a modest business. We are debating whether extreme inherited wealth should be allowed to pass untouched through the generations.”

That is important. The strongest “for” position is **not** “tax all inheritance.” It is:

> “Tax the very top, because extreme wealth has a different social meaning than ordinary private wealth.”

## Why “really big estates” matters

If you want to sound credible, emphasize the threshold. Say something like:

> “This is not about people who inherit their parents’ house. It is about estates so large that they can fund lifestyles across generations without work. That is where the social problem begins.”

That neutralizes a lot of opposition. Many people who oppose inheritance tax in general are not actually defending huge dynastic fortunes; they are defending their own family home, their small business, or their parents’ pension.

Your side should be clear:

> “If the proposal targets only very large estates, it is legitimate. If it hits ordinary families, then no.”

But since your debate question is about “really big estates,” you can confidently say: **yes.**

## Best points to make

### 1. Equality of opportunity

Switzerland likes to say it is meritocratic. But if one group of people can be born into enormous financial security while others have to fight from scratch, that weakens meritocracy.

Say:

> “A society that calls itself meritocratic should not allow wealth to be transferred in such a way that talent and hard work matter less than birth.”

You do not need to say “take everything from the rich.” Just:

> “A modest but meaningful contribution from extreme inherited wealth helps reduce the gap between winners by effort and winners by birth.”

### 2. Democratic legitimacy

Extreme wealth concentration can make political and social systems feel unequal. Even if the rich are legally protected, the perception of a “two-class society” is politically damaging.

Say:

> “When wealth is passed on in huge amounts without any corresponding contribution to the community, it undermines the idea that society is a shared project.”

A federal tax on extreme estates is a way of saying:

> “The state is not just a tax-collecting machine. It is the shared framework that protects property, contracts, education, and old-age security.”

### 3. Federalism as a reason for, not against, a federal tax

The “against” side may say: “Switzerland is federal; taxes should be left to the cantons.”

Your answer:

> “Federalism exists to protect diversity, but it should not become a race to the bottom for the very rich. If cantons compete by lowering inheritance taxes on enormous estates, that is not healthy federalism; it is fiscal arbitrage.”

A federal tax on extreme estates can:

- prevent cantonal tax competition at the top,
- ensure a minimum level of social contribution,
- avoid situations where very wealthy families simply choose the most favorable canton.

Say:

> “Federalism should mean diversity, not a bidding war to attract extreme wealth.”

### 4. It can be designed to avoid harm

This is very important for credibility. You should not sound like you want to destroy family businesses or force liquidations.

Say:

> “A well-designed inheritance tax on large estates would include safeguards: liquidity relief, exemptions for family businesses where needed, and a high threshold so that only extreme estates are affected.”

This makes you look reasonable, not ideological.

### 5. It is not the main driver of economic success

The other side will say: “If you tax inheritance, you drive wealth away from Switzerland.”

Your answer:

> “Capital is mobile, but Switzerland’s competitiveness is not based only on low inheritance tax. It is based on stable institutions, skilled people, security of property, quality education, infrastructure, and a functioning social state.”

Then:

> “We should not sacrifice social cohesion just to keep a symbolic tax advantage for a tiny group of extremely wealthy families.”

## Rebuttals to expect

### “That will lead to capital flight.”

Answer:

> “Maybe a few very wealthy families will move, but if a society wants to protect social cohesion, it should not structure its entire system around the relocation threats of a tiny elite. Moreover, a tax only on extreme inheritances is less likely to distort decisions than income or corporate taxes.”

### “It double-taxes wealth.”

Answer:

> “The wealth was likely earned, taxed, and then inherited. A federal tax on extreme estates at the point of transfer is not irrational. It targets the intergenerational transfer itself, especially where the inherited amount is large enough to create structural advantage.”

Better version:

> “If the system is designed well, it can avoid excessive double taxation by coordinating with cantonal inheritance taxes.”

### “It hurts family businesses.”

Answer:

> “That is why the threshold should be high and the design should include safeguards. A tax on extreme estates is not the same as a death tax on small businesses. If family businesses are protected where appropriate, that objection weakens.”

### “Switzerland is federal; this is not the right level.”

Answer:

> “That is exactly why it should be federal if we want to stop cantonal competition at the very top. Otherwise, the wealthy can play cantons against each other.”

### “Rich people create wealth; we should not tax them.”

Answer:

> “Creating wealth is legitimate. But passing enormous wealth down through generations without any social contribution is a different question. We are not taxing their earnings; we are asking whether extreme inherited wealth should also have a duty to society.”

## Strong closing argument

End with something simple and memorable:

> “Switzerland is rich. It is stable. It is free. But a country that allows extreme wealth to be passed on untouched, generation after generation, is also a country where birth matters too much. A federal inheritance tax on very large estates would not destroy Swiss wealth. It would remind us that wealth is part of society, not above it.”

Or:

> “If we do not tax extreme inherited wealth, the alternative is not fairness. It is dynastic privilege.”

## My honest verdict

If the initiative is about a **federal inheritance tax on really big estates only**, I would support it.

Not because I think inheritance tax solves everything. But because, in a country with high wealth inequality and strong federalism, a narrow federal tax on extreme estates is one of the few tools that can:

- reduce dynastic inequality,
- improve social cohesion,
- finance shared old-age and social infrastructure,
- and prevent cantonal tax competition at the very top.

**Bottom line: yes, Switzerland should do it — but only if the threshold is high enough that it is truly about extreme wealth, not ordinary families.**
